name: Ivermectin cream

lead: Ivermectin 1% cream (Soolantra) is a prescription topical approved for papulopustular rosacea. People use it to reduce the red bumps and pustules on the face and get a calmer, clearer look.

It is thought to act on Demodex mites and to lower inflammatory signals such as LL-37 and KLK5 in skin models. A large Phase 3 trial compared it with metronidazole cream, and a systematic review and meta-analysis examined its efficacy and quality-of-life impact.

paras: It is applied to the face once daily as a prescribed treatment, often long-term as part of a rosacea routine alongside sun protection and gentle skincare.
Adverse-event details are in the trial and label data. It is a prescription topical, distinct from oral ivermectin.

angle.text: Ivermectin cream is a prescription treatment used to reduce the red bumps of papulopustular rosacea for a calmer-looking face. It acts on Demodex mites and skin inflammation, and Phase 3 trials support its approved use.

lead: Ivermectin 1% (10 mg/g) cream, marketed as Soolantra, is a prescription topical approved for the inflammatory bumps and pimples of papulopustular rosacea.[1][2] It is applied once daily to the face, and people use it to reduce the red papules and pustules that change the look of the cheeks, nose, chin and forehead.[2][3]

Rosacea lesions can look like acne, and reviews note that the condition affects self-esteem and quality of life.[4] Treatment is aimed at calming the lesions so facial skin looks clearer and less inflamed; in trials, participants also reported improved skin-related quality of life.[5]

Researchers have proposed that the drug acts both against Demodex mites, which live in facial follicles and are suspected to contribute to rosacea, and through anti-inflammatory effects; laboratory work found it reduced expression of the innate-immune mediators LL-37 and KLK5 in skin models.[6][7] Phase 3 trials compared it with vehicle and with metronidazole cream, and a systematic review and meta-analysis examined its efficacy and quality-of-life impact.[1][8][4]
Ivermectin itself was discovered as an antiparasitic drug, and the topical rosacea cream is a separate prescription product from oral ivermectin.[9]

paras: Papulopustular rosacea shows up as persistent facial redness with dome-shaped bumps and pustules. Topical ivermectin is used to lower the number of these inflammatory lesions, which is the most visible part of the condition.[2][1] Reviews describe it as a convenient once-daily option compared with older twice-daily topicals.[1]

Topical ivermectin is indicated for inflammatory lesions of rosacea.[2][3] Case series and small studies have also looked at ocular rosacea and Demodex infestation of the eyelids.[8][10] A randomized study published in 2024 examined topical ivermectin for inflamed rhinophyma, the nose thickening that can accompany advanced rosacea.[11]

It has been described as complementary to oral modified-release doxycycline 40 mg, since the two target different inflammatory pathways, and a 2026 split-face trial examined whether adding ivermectin cream improved KTP laser treatment of rosacea redness.[12][13]

Ivermectin belongs to the avermectin family of macrocyclic lactones, which are broad-spectrum antiparasitic agents that also show anti-inflammatory properties.[1] Rosacea involves elevated cathelicidin peptides such as LL-37 and the protease KLK5 that cleaves them; ivermectin cream reduced their gene expression in reconstructed and ex vivo skin models.[6]

The cause of papulopustular rosacea is not fully understood. Reviews describe involvement of innate and adaptive immune responses and possible contribution from Demodex mites, which is why a drug with both antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory effects has drawn interest.[2][7]

In pooled phase 3 data summarised in one review, the most common treatment-related adverse events were skin burning sensation, itching, dry skin and skin irritation, each occurring in fewer than 2 percent of participants, and the cream was described as well tolerated.[1] Reviews of the product label-level information are available in drug bulletins and family-medicine summaries.[3][14]

Ivermectin was developed from avermectins discovered in a soil bacterium, Streptomyces avermitilis, isolated by Satoshi Omura and studied by William Campbell; the two shared part of the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on parasitic disease.[9] The topical cream for rosacea was reviewed in the medical literature as a new agent in 2015.[1][14]

In phase 3 trials of 12 or 16 weeks in adults with moderate to severe papulopustular rosacea, once-daily ivermectin 1% cream improved Investigator Global Assessment scores and inflammatory lesion counts versus vehicle and was more effective than twice-daily metronidazole 0.75% cream; extension studies reported continued benefit for up to 52 weeks.[1] One of the registered comparisons enrolled 962 participants.[15]

A randomized trial analysis reported improved health-related quality of life with ivermectin cream.[5] A systematic review and meta-analysis assessed topical ivermectin 1% against other topicals on efficacy and quality of life, noting a shortage of head-to-head high-quality evidence.[4] A 34-patient case series reported results from clinical practice.[16]

Additional registered trials cover bioequivalence of generic creams, Demodex-related conditions and ocular Demodex.[17][18] A review of emerging rosacea therapies places topical ivermectin among established options.[19]

No looksmaxxing-forum discussion of the cream is cited here. It is a dermatologist-prescribed product and is separate from public debates over oral ivermectin use, which concern different indications.

timeline.event: Satoshi Omura isolates the avermectin-producing bacterium from Japanese soil.[9]
Phase 3 comparison of ivermectin 1% cream and metronidazole 0.75% cream in papulopustular rosacea begins.[15]
Reviews introduce ivermectin 1% cream as a new once-daily rosacea topical; Omura and Campbell share the Nobel Prize.[1][9]
